w: What's tested How a "functional disturbance" happens: normal function plus an event that's more than you can tolerate gives symptoms What a TMD is, and why it isn't one thing The five causes: how the jaw and teeth fit, trauma, stress, deep pain and habits like grinding What the evidence says about bite problems and TMD, and why grinding teeth "just in case" isn't done Treatments: reversible first (splints), irreversible only when the bite is the cause Loose teeth and worn teeth: what's normal, what isn't, and the kinds of wear Grinding at night: it starts in the brain, not the bite, and a splint protects the teeth This lecture (10/29) switches direction: instead of how occlusion works, it's about when things go wrong, why, and what we do. It sets up the TMD course in third year. Sometimes the bite has nothing to do with the problem; other times, working on the bite still helps the patient get better. Dr. Givan said to learn the general themes here; the details of each jaw disorder come next year. Normal function and dysfunction The jaw's normal jobs are chewing, swallowing and speaking. Dysfunction means those jobs are changed or blocked: you can't move the way you should, or it hurts. The cause of dysfunction is called a functional disturbance, and often we never find out why it started. Examples: muscle problems (you can't open as wide; the bite suddenly feels "off" because a muscle's resting length changed), joint changes (the jaw swings to one side as it opens), too much force on the teeth (broken teeth, tooth pain, bone loss, wear), and headaches (there are over 250 kinds). What a TMD is People say "I have TMJ," but TMJ is the joint. The problem is a temporomandibular disorder, or TMD: an umbrella word for many different problems of the chewing muscles, the jaw joint, or both. Most change how the jaw works, and some hurt. About half are in the muscles, about a third in the joints, and the rest elsewhere, often mixed. There are more than 40 of them, each diagnosed and treated differently, so "I'm being treated for TMD" tells you almost nothing. The slides use Bell's classification. Many TMDs have nothing to do with the bite. A TMD is also not the same as orofacial pain, which is a much bigger group of head and neck pains. Dentists have long blamed the bite for TMD. Today Dr. Givan says it differently: bite treatments can create an environment for healing, which helps, but that doesn't mean the bite caused the problem. How a problem starts The model is: normal function + an event, more than your tolerance → symptoms. Normal function is run by the brainstem (learned patterns), adjusted by feedback from the mouth and by the emotional brain. An event can be local, like a high crown, a burn from hot pizza, a strain, grinding or ongoing pain, or body-wide, like stress or illness. Your tolerance depends on local things (how your bite places your jaw, and whether the joints sit stably) and body-wide things (genes, gender, diet, disease). If the total stays under your tolerance, you adapt and feel nothing. If it goes over, symptoms start. Any part can change, so something you handled fine yesterday may be too much today. That's the typical TMD story: fine for years, then one Tuesday, terrible pain. When the system breaks down you can see: tooth pain (pulpitis), worn or broken teeth, loose teeth, sore chewing muscles, jaw joint pain, ear pain and headaches. The five causes 1. How the jaw and teeth fit (mandibular stability), 2. trauma, 3. emotional stress, 4. deep pain, 5. habits like clenching and grinding (parafunction). He spent the most time on the first, because it's the one dentists control. 1. How well the jaw and teeth fit Mandibular stability means the teeth and both joints fit against the skull at the same time. The research linking bite and TMD is weak, partly because studies rarely say which TMD they looked at. Pullinger and Seligman found these more often in TMD patients: a skeletal open bite in front, a slide of more than 2 mm from the first contact (joints seated) into the full bite, more than 4 mm of overjet, and five or more missing back teeth. But people without TMD have them too, so they concluded the bite isn't the most important factor. In a review of 57 studies, 22 found no link and 35 found some link, and a link doesn't prove cause. Still, everyone agrees a good bite is the base of good dentistry: all teeth touching evenly at once, forces straight down the teeth, front teeth separating the back teeth when you move. Ideally the joints are fully seated (orthopedic stability) and the teeth fully together (occlusal stability). The five treatment goals: joints up and forward against the slope, discs in place between joint and socket, back teeth touching evenly with forces down the long axis, front teeth separating the back teeth in movements, and in the head-forward eating posture, slightly heavier back contacts than front. The catch: only about 10% of people can close with their joints seated straight into their best bite. For everyone else, getting the teeth together pulls one or both joints off their seat. That's orthopedic instability, and it can lead to a problem inside the joint (an intracapsular disorder). The risk goes up with the size of the gap (1-2 mm usually isn't a problem; more than 3 mm raises the risk) and with heavy force, as in people who grind. Open bites and Class II bites have been linked to TMD, but not strongly. His example: a patient in severe pain who had had lots of crowns and bridges over the years. Each one fit her teeth but pulled her jaw a little farther from its seated position, until one day she couldn't tolerate it. A full-coverage splint let her joints settle back, which opened a gap between her front teeth. She was rebuilt at that new position, in temporaries for over a year, about two years in all, and her pain was relieved. In her case the bite really was the problem. 2. The bite and the muscles Bite something hard by surprise and your jaw pops open: a fast, automatic protective reflex in the brainstem. Studies of muscle activity showed that when back teeth don't touch, the closing muscles relax, and when the back molars touch, the muscles fire fully. So back-tooth contact turns the closing muscles on. Removing non-working side contacts keeps the masseter and temporalis quiet in that movement, which is one argument for canine guidance. Normal function (ortho-function) uses this feedback. Parafunction (clenching, grinding, habits) doesn't: the muscles fight each other, tighten up and get tired and strained, and tooth contacts don't start it. The high crown. Leave a new crown slightly high and the patient starts guarding: moving the jaw stiffly to avoid hitting it. That's protective co-contraction. It's a normal response, not a disease, but moving that way makes the muscles sore. Here the bite did cause a muscle problem. But bite "interferences" a patient already has (non-working or working side contacts on back teeth) show up just as often in people with no symptoms. A slide under 2 mm is equally common in both groups; over 2 mm is more common in patients with symptoms. So: adding an interference can cause problems, removing old ones doesn't seem to help TMD, and grinding someone's teeth to prevent TMD isn't supported. Don't build a new non-working contact into a crown, but don't grind away one that's always been there. In short: sudden changes cause guarding, but people usually adapt once it's fixed. Joint instability has to be large, and needs heavy force, to matter. And an old, harmless problem can become a problem when the tolerance drops: the straw that broke the camel's back. A rule of thumb: trouble moving the jaw is usually the muscles; pain once the teeth are together is usually the joints. Treatments Occlusal therapy is anything that changes the bite. Reversible treatments: education, physical therapy, medication, counseling and a flat plane stabilization splint, the only one of these that changes the bite. Irreversible treatments: adjusting (grinding) the teeth, restorations, a repositioning splint, orthodontics, jaw surgery and joint surgery. A splint is a plastic cover over the biting surfaces with a new, ideal bite built on it, so the joints can sit seated. It helps sore muscles, protects teeth and crowns, eases joint pain and works as a trial treatment. It is "hugely effective." A stabilizing splint keeps the joints seated; a repositioning splint holds the jaw in a different, chosen position (for some disc problems or sleep apnea). Other names: night guard, occlusal device or appliance, bite plate. An upper splint has a flat back surface and a ramp in front. It's very stable, tough and easy to adjust, works for any bite class, and is best for a Class II division 1 bite with a big overjet; it's usually worn at night. A lower splint gets in the way of speech less and shows less, so it's better for daytime. Full coverage (all the teeth) is recommended almost always. Partial coverage can push covered teeth in and let uncovered teeth drift out, may work less well, and small ones can be swallowed at night. Most irreversible dental work is just normal dentistry for broken or decayed teeth. But for a patient with a functional disturbance, do something permanent only when there's good reason to think the bite is the main cause, and do the least you can. How much depends on how far off the bite is: the rule of thirds. Within the first third of the tooth, adjust the enamel (remove first contacts, remove interferences, make forces go straight down, then perfect the bite; never into dentin). In the middle third, crowns and minor orthodontics. Beyond that, major orthodontics, jaw surgery and crowns. Reversible and irreversible treatments have about the same long-term success, 50-90%, so start conservative, and go further only if that fails. Also weigh symptoms, the teeth's condition, health, looks and cost. 3. Trauma "A force is only traumatic when it causes trauma." Five things decide that: how strong, how often, how long, which direction (sideways is worse than straight down) and how many teeth share it. Macrotrauma is a sudden big force, like a car crash; microtrauma is small repeated force, like grinding. Results include a broken jaw, joint damage and damage to teeth: cracks, looseness and wear. Inside, the ligament and bone around the tooth change; you see loose or drifting teeth, wear, a wider ligament space on x-ray, tenderness and tooth pain. Force damages the attachment around the root, rarely the gums. Loose teeth A healthy tooth doesn't visibly move up and down, but it does sink about 28 microns when you bite, front or back. It springs back about 7 microns right away and takes about 4 hours to fully recover. An implant moves only 2-3 microns under 10 pounds. Side-to-side movement is always bigger. Single-root teeth move more than multi-root teeth. About 500 grams of push moves a tooth 56-108 microns; up to 150 microns is normal, more than that is not. Teeth are loosest when you wake up and tightest late in the day. Adapted looseness stays the same and can last for years without harm. Traumatic looseness keeps getting worse, and that's when teeth are splinted together. You can only tell them apart by checking over time. Miller's index: 0 no movement, 1 barely noticeable, 2 sideways up to 1 mm, 3 more than 1 mm or pushing down or turning. Worn teeth Some wear is normal for age; the same wear at 30 isn't. Wear rarely hurts, so patients usually come in because of looks, often late. Treat it before it spreads to many teeth; the canines and front teeth that guide the jaw wear first. Badly worn teeth may need gum surgery, root canals or orthodontic pulling-up before crowns, unless 3 mm of tooth shows above the gum point between teeth. The four kinds: attrition is tooth-on-tooth grinding (shiny, sharp-edged spots that match the opposite tooth); abrasion is wear from something in between, most often a toothbrush; erosion is acid (dull, cupped-out surfaces, with fillings left standing above the tooth); abfraction is the idea that flexing under bite force chips notches near the gumline. Acid speeds up the other kinds. Acid patterns: reflux (GERD) erodes the tongue side of all the upper teeth and the tops of the lower molars, often worse on the side the person sleeps on. Bulimia mostly erodes the upper front teeth, and can destroy them while the lower front teeth are spared. Soda: swishing gives all-over satin erosion; holding it at the back is severe, with lots of cavities. Sucking lemons makes front teeth look like screwdriver tips. Also drugs, chlorinated pools and battery or galvanizing work. Notches at the gumline (noncarious cervical lesions) are very common, more so with age, most often on the cheek side of upper premolars. They are rounded saucers or sharp V-notches, usually without decay. They're filled with composite only when needed (growing, sensitive, unsightly, trapping food). Their cause is mixed: hard sideways brushing, acid and reflux, with the bite involved but not enough on its own. Abfraction works in the lab but hasn't been proven in patients, so it isn't counted as a main type of wear. Clenching and nail biting are linked to these notches more than grinding is. 3 and 4. Stress and deep pain Stress works through the brain's emotional centers, which tighten the muscle sensors (spindles) so muscles, especially in the head and neck, stay tense and hurt more easily. Deep pain (below the skin or gums) is easy to miss: a bad tooth can limit opening, and fixing the tooth brings the opening back. Neck pain can affect the jaw too. 5. Clenching, grinding and other habits These habits are outside normal function and mostly unconscious, so they're hard to control. Daytime: clenching (look for chipped, broken or splayed teeth and bony bumps called tori), grinding, cheek or tongue biting, thumb sucking, odd postures, chewing pens or nails, holding a phone or violin under the chin. Nighttime: bruxism (rhythmic clenching and grinding in sleep), pushing the tongue against the teeth (a scalloped tongue edge), cheek biting. Bruxism is very damaging: the forces are 3-5 times normal, sideways, in any jaw position, and the protective reflexes are off while you sleep. Sleep is about 80% non-REM and 20% REM. Grinding starts when sleep gets lighter; in sleep labs, lights or sounds can trigger it. Most events last 5-10 seconds, many times a night. Bruxism starts in the brain, more like restless legs than a bite problem. It's linked to oxygen levels (sleep apnea), stress, medications and genes. The bite doesn't start it. The main treatment is a stabilization splint: grinding stops for a while, then comes back, so the point is to grind on the splint instead of the teeth ("the $400 splint instead of the $40,000 rehab"). Sleeping on your side, managing stress, less alcohol, quitting smoking, hypnosis and acupuncture are also suggested, with little proof. Studies showed nighttime jaw muscle activity going up with stressful events (a job interview, a fight, quitting a job) and down on vacation, along with pain. That's why TMD care involves other health professionals. Children often grind, usually without symptoms, as their changing teeth look for a stable bite. Tell parents it's usually harmless and to watch it; see a dentist if chewing is affected. The big picture: the bite matters in a few of these problems, but most have nothing to do with it. Even so, a simple splint often helps them heal. It treats the symptoms, not the cause.
